oneLine: 1 Timothy is a short letter of advice and instruction to Timothy, a younger church leader, about how a Christian community should live, worship and choose its leaders.
writtenBy: The letter names the apostle Paul as its author. An apostle was one of the early leaders sent out to spread the message about Jesus. Christians traditionally accepted Paul as the writer. Many modern scholars think a later follower of Paul wrote it in his name, because its vocabulary, style and picture of church life differ from Paul's undisputed letters. Others still defend Paul as the author, so this remains an open and widely debated question.
when: If Paul wrote it, it probably dates to the 60s AD, near the end of his life, while he was travelling and Timothy had stayed behind in the city of Ephesus, in what is now western Turkey. Scholars who think it came from a later writer usually place it in the late first or early second century. Either way, it comes from a time when small groups of Christians were learning how to organise themselves.
writtenTo: Timothy, a younger coworker of Paul who appears in the book of Acts and in several of Paul's letters. The letter says he was left in Ephesus to guide the church there. Its closing greeting is addressed to more than one person, which suggests it was also meant to be read by the wider community.
why: The letter says some people in the church were spreading teaching that led others away from love, honesty and a clear conscience, and it urges Timothy to stand against this. It gives practical guidance on prayer, leadership, caring for widows and handling money. In the Bible's bigger story it shows the early church moving from its first missionary days toward settled communities. Running through it is a short summary of the Christian message: that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and that the writer counts himself as the clearest example of that mercy.
themes: Caring for people with no one else to support them
Contentment and the danger of loving money

outline.label: Warning about false teaching and a story of mercy
Prayer and order when the church gathers

Money, contentment and a final charge

readingTip: Read it as a real letter between two coworkers. We only hear one side, so the false teaching it opposes is hinted at rather than explained, and scholars still debate exactly what it was. Some passages, especially the instructions about women in chapter 2 and about slaves in chapter 6, reflect the household customs of the ancient world. Christians today disagree strongly about how they should apply now, so it helps to notice the setting and read them alongside the rest of the Bible.
